passages.t: Hands held out all day long
passages.happening:
God answers the prayer. ‘I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me; I was found by those who did not seek Me’ (verse 1). To a nation that did not call on his name, he kept saying that he was there (verse 1).

‘All day long I have held out My hands to an obstinate people who walk in the wrong path, who follow their own imaginations’ (verse 2). They provoke him to his face, sacrificing in gardens and burning incense on altars of brick (verse 3). They sit among the graves and spend nights in secret places, and eat pork and unclean broth (verse 4). They tell others to keep away, claiming to be holier than everyone else (verse 5). ‘Such people are smoke in My nostrils, a fire that burns all day long’ (verse 5).

God will not keep silent. He will repay, both for their iniquities and for those of their fathers, who burned incense on the mountains and scorned him on the hills (verses 6 and 7).
passages.hearers:
In 63:7 to 64:12 the people asked why God was silent and hidden. Chapter 65 is his reply, and it turns the question around. God has not been hiding. He has been saying he is there to people who did not look for him, and holding out his hands to people who would not take them.

The rites named in verses 3 to 5 were all forbidden by the law. Sacrifice in gardens points to sacred groves linked with fertility religion. Altars of brick broke the command that altars be made of earth or uncut stone. Sitting among graves and spending nights in secret places suggests seeking the dead or seeking dreams from spirits. Pork and unclean broth broke the food laws. And the claim to be holier than others shows people who thought these rites made them specially sacred.

Many scholars place the chapter among the returned community in the late sixth or early fifth century BC; those who hold to one author read it as Isaiah's prophecy of a divided people to come. The sharp line it draws may reflect real tensions in Judah after the return, also seen in Ezra, Nehemiah and Malachi.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 1 of Gentiles who came to faith, ‘I was found by those who did not seek Me’ (Romans 10:20), and verse 2 of his own people (Romans 10:21). In Romans 11 he goes on to say that God has not rejected his people.
passages.hard:
Paul applies verse 2, hands held out to an obstinate people, to Israel in his own day. Does that give anyone reason to blame the Jewish people?

No. In Isaiah the verse is God's word to his own people, spoken by an Israelite prophet, and the same chapter keeps a faithful remnant within Israel (verses 8 and 9). Paul, himself a Jew, quotes it while grieving for his own people, and in the next chapter he insists that God has not rejected them (Romans 11:1-2). The obstinacy the verse describes is found in every people, the church included.

The chapter's division is between those who seek God and those who forsake him, and it runs through every people. It gives no one a warrant for contempt toward the Jewish people.
passages.asks: God says he held out his hands all day long to people who did not take them. Ask whether you are among those he has been reaching for. And ask whether any of your religious habits make you feel holier than others, as verse 5 describes.

passages.t: A cluster not destroyed, and two destinies
passages.happening:
‘This is what the LORD says’ (verse 8). When new wine is found in a cluster of grapes, people say not to destroy it because there is good in it. So God will act for his servants and not destroy them all (verse 8). He will bring descendants from Jacob and heirs from Judah to possess his mountains (verse 9). Sharon will be a pasture for flocks and the Valley of Achor a resting place for herds, for those who seek him (verse 10).

But those who forsake the LORD, who set a table for Fortune and fill bowls of wine for Destiny, God will destine for the sword (verses 11 and 12), ‘because I called and you did not answer, I spoke and you did not listen’ (verse 12).

Then a series of reversals. ‘My servants will eat, but you will go hungry; My servants will drink, but you will go thirsty’ (verse 13). His servants will shout for joy while the others wail (verse 14). To his servants he will give another name (verse 15). Whoever swears in the land will swear by the God of truth, for the former troubles will be forgotten (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
A farmer does not throw away a whole bunch of grapes because some are bad, if there is still good juice in it. God will not destroy the whole people. The faithful within it will live.

The word servants appears seven times in this chapter. In chapters 40 to 53 the word was almost always singular, the Servant who suffers for others. From chapter 54 on it is plural: those who share the Servant's faith and inherit what he won.

The Sharon is the fertile plain on the west coast. The Valley of Achor lies near Jericho on the east, where Achan was stoned after Jericho fell. Hosea had promised it would become a door of hope. From the sea to the Jordan, the land will be pasture again.

Fortune, Gad, was a god of luck known across the region, and Destiny, Meni, a god of fate. A table and bowls of mixed wine describe a sacred meal set for them. The next verse makes a pun: those who pour for Destiny will be destined, manah, for the sword.

In verse 16 God is called the God of truth, literally the God of Amen, whose word is firm.
passages.later: Hosea had promised to ‘make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope’ (Hosea 2:15). And the Valley of Achor is where Achan's story ended (Joshua 7:24-26).
passages.asks: God keeps the cluster because there is still good in it. Ask whether you see in your church or family what God sees in a cluster of grapes. And ask whether the name you will leave behind is one that calls on the God of truth.

passages.t: New heavens and a new earth
passages.happening:
‘For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind’ (verse 17). ‘But be glad and rejoice forever in what I create; for I will create Jerusalem to be a joy and its people to be a delight’ (verse 18). ‘The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her’ (verse 19).

No longer will an infant live only a few days, or an old man fail to live out his years. Someone who dies at a hundred will be thought young (verse 20). ‘They will build houses and dwell in them; they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit’ (verse 21). No one will build for others to live in or plant for others to eat (verse 22). They will not labor in vain or bear children doomed to disaster (verse 23).

‘Even before they call, I will answer, and while they are still speaking, I will hear’ (verse 24). ‘The wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox, but the food of the serpent will be dust’ (verse 25). They will neither harm nor destroy on all God's holy mountain (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The vision widens to a whole new creation. The verb create, bara, used three times in verses 17 and 18, is the verb kept for God's own acts and used in the Bible's first verse. The future is as fresh and divine as the first creation.

The new creation undoes the old curses one by one: early death, work stolen by others, children born to disaster, prayer that seems unheard. The first hearers knew all of them. Their houses had been taken, their harvests eaten by others, their children lost.

Verse 25 squeezes the peaceable kingdom of 11:6-9 into one line and adds that the serpent's food will be dust, an echo of the curse in Genesis 3. The enemy of the first garden is kept down for good.
passages.later: Peter writes, ‘we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells’ (2 Peter 3:13). Revelation sees ‘a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away’ (Revelation 21:1), where there will be no more mourning or crying.
passages.hard:
If there is no more death in the new creation, why does verse 20 speak of people dying at a hundred?

Revelation 21:4 says there will be no more death, yet verse 20 speaks of the young dying at a hundred. Readers have taken it in three main ways. Many premillennial interpreters see verses 20 to 25 as an earthly thousand-year reign of Christ before the final state (Revelation 20), a time of long life and peace in which death and sin still exist but are held back. Many amillennial and postmillennial interpreters, with many Old Testament scholars, read it as poetry describing an unimaginable future in the best terms the first hearers knew: long life, fruitful work, safe children. A third view ties it first to the restoration of Jerusalem after the exile, as a foretaste of something greater.

These readings differ on the millennium, a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree. All agree that the chapter promises a real renewed world, not a bodiless heaven, and that God means to end weeping and wasted life.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God promises a world where no one labors in vain. Ask what work of yours feels wasted, and whether you can hope for it in this promise. And ask what it would mean to live now as someone who expects the wolf and the lamb to feed together.
